brain.name: Brain
brain.location: The entire central organ of the nervous system, enclosed within the skull.
brain.summary: The brain integrates sensory information, controls voluntary and involuntary actions, and is the seat of cognition, emotion, and memory.

cerebrum.name: Cerebrum
cerebrum.location: The largest part of the brain, forming its upper and outer bulk, divided into left and right hemispheres.
cerebrum.summary: Responsible for higher-order functions including voluntary movement, sensory perception, language, and abstract thought. Its surface (the cerebral cortex) is highly folded to increase surface area.

frontal_lobe.name: Frontal Lobe
frontal_lobe.location: The most anterior lobe of the cerebrum, in front of the central sulcus.
frontal_lobe.summary: Governs voluntary motor control, executive function, and behavior regulation. Contains the primary motor cortex and prefrontal cortex.
functions: Expressive language (Broca's area, typically left hemisphere)
frontal_lobe.clinicalRelevance: Frontal lobe damage is classically associated with changes in personality and impulse control — the 19th-century case of Phineas Gage is the textbook example. Educational note, not a diagnostic claim.

parietal_lobe.name: Parietal Lobe
parietal_lobe.location: Posterior to the frontal lobe and superior to the temporal lobe.
parietal_lobe.summary: Processes somatosensory information — touch, temperature, pain, and body position — and contributes to spatial awareness.

temporal_lobe.name: Temporal Lobe
temporal_lobe.location: Below the lateral (Sylvian) fissure, on the lower sides of the cerebrum.
temporal_lobe.summary: Central to auditory processing, language comprehension, and memory; contains the hippocampus.
functions: Language comprehension (Wernicke's area, typically left hemisphere)

occipital_lobe.name: Occipital Lobe
occipital_lobe.location: The most posterior lobe of the cerebrum, at the back of the skull.
occipital_lobe.summary: The brain's primary visual processing center.

cerebellum.name: Cerebellum
cerebellum.location: Beneath the occipital lobe and behind the brainstem, at the back and base of the skull.
cerebellum.summary: Coordinates voluntary movement, balance, and motor learning. Despite its small size, it contains most of the brain's neurons.
functions: Fine-tuning of movement precision and timing
Contributions to some cognitive and language processing
cerebellum.clinicalRelevance: Cerebellar damage classically produces ataxia (uncoordinated movement) without paralysis. Educational note, not a diagnostic claim.

brainstem.name: Brainstem
brainstem.location: Connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord; made up of the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata.
brainstem.summary: Controls many of the body's automatic, life-sustaining functions and relays signals between the brain and the rest of the body.
functions: Regulation of breathing and heart rate
Relay of motor and sensory signals
Regulation of consciousness and arousal (reticular formation)
brainstem.clinicalRelevance: Brainstem injury is uniquely life-threatening because it houses the centers controlling breathing and cardiovascular function. Educational note, not a diagnostic claim.

corpus_callosum.name: Corpus Callosum
corpus_callosum.location: A broad band of white matter beneath the cerebral cortex, spanning the midline between the hemispheres.
corpus_callosum.summary: The largest white matter structure in the brain; connects and allows communication between the left and right cerebral hemispheres.
functions: Coordination of bilateral movement and sensation

hypothalamus.name: Hypothalamus
hypothalamus.location: Below the thalamus and above the brainstem, forming the floor of the third ventricle.
hypothalamus.summary: A small but critical structure that links the nervous system to the endocrine system via the pituitary gland.
functions: Control of the pituitary gland and hormone release
Regulation of circadian rhythms and sleep

third_ventricle.name: Third Ventricle
third_ventricle.location: A narrow, midline cavity between the two halves of the thalamus.
third_ventricle.summary: One of the brain's four interconnected ventricles; part of the system that produces and circulates cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

fourth_ventricle.name: Fourth Ventricle
fourth_ventricle.location: Located between the brainstem (pons and medulla) and the cerebellum.
fourth_ventricle.summary: The most inferior of the brain's ventricles; connects to the central canal of the spinal cord.
functions: Connects the ventricular system to the spinal cord's central canal

thalamus_left.name: Left Thalamus
thalamus_left.location: A paired, egg-shaped structure deep in the brain, just above the brainstem.
thalamus_left.summary: The brain's primary sensory relay station; nearly all sensory information (except smell) passes through the thalamus before reaching the cortex.
functions: Relay of sensory information to the cortex

thalamus_right.name: Right Thalamus
thalamus_right.location: A paired, egg-shaped structure deep in the brain, just above the brainstem.
thalamus_right.summary: The brain's primary sensory relay station; nearly all sensory information (except smell) passes through the thalamus before reaching the cortex.
functions: Relay of sensory information to the cortex

hippocampus_left.name: Left Hippocampus
hippocampus_left.location: A curled structure deep within the temporal lobe, part of the limbic system.
hippocampus_left.summary: Essential for forming new long-term memories and for spatial navigation.
functions: Consolidation of memories from short-term to long-term storage
hippocampus_left.clinicalRelevance: The hippocampus is among the first regions affected in Alzheimer's disease, which is part of why early memory loss is a hallmark symptom. Educational note, not a diagnostic claim.

hippocampus_right.name: Right Hippocampus
hippocampus_right.location: A curled structure deep within the temporal lobe, part of the limbic system.
hippocampus_right.summary: Essential for forming new long-term memories and for spatial navigation.
functions: Consolidation of memories from short-term to long-term storage
hippocampus_right.clinicalRelevance: The hippocampus is among the first regions affected in Alzheimer's disease, which is part of why early memory loss is a hallmark symptom. Educational note, not a diagnostic claim.

amygdala_left.name: Left Amygdala
amygdala_left.location: An almond-shaped structure just anterior to the hippocampus, in the medial temporal lobe.
amygdala_left.summary: Central to processing emotions, particularly fear and threat detection.
functions: Emotional processing, especially fear and threat response
Modulation of memory consolidation for emotionally significant events

amygdala_right.name: Right Amygdala
amygdala_right.location: An almond-shaped structure just anterior to the hippocampus, in the medial temporal lobe.
amygdala_right.summary: Central to processing emotions, particularly fear and threat detection.
functions: Emotional processing, especially fear and threat response
Modulation of memory consolidation for emotionally significant events

caudate_nucleus_left.name: Left Caudate Nucleus
caudate_nucleus_left.location: A C-shaped structure deep within the cerebrum, part of the basal ganglia.
caudate_nucleus_left.summary: Involved in voluntary movement regulation and several cognitive processes, working together with the putamen as the striatum.

caudate_nucleus_right.name: Right Caudate Nucleus
caudate_nucleus_right.location: A C-shaped structure deep within the cerebrum, part of the basal ganglia.
caudate_nucleus_right.summary: Involved in voluntary movement regulation and several cognitive processes, working together with the putamen as the striatum.

putamen_left.name: Left Putamen
putamen_left.location: Part of the basal ganglia, lateral to the globus pallidus.
putamen_left.summary: Works together with the caudate nucleus (forming the striatum) to regulate movement.
functions: Some contribution to reinforcement and reward processing

putamen_right.name: Right Putamen
putamen_right.location: Part of the basal ganglia, lateral to the globus pallidus.
putamen_right.summary: Works together with the caudate nucleus (forming the striatum) to regulate movement.
functions: Some contribution to reinforcement and reward processing

globus_pallidus_left.name: Left Globus Pallidus
globus_pallidus_left.location: Deep within the cerebrum, medial to the putamen, part of the basal ganglia.
globus_pallidus_left.summary: A key output structure of the basal ganglia motor circuit.
functions: Part of the basal ganglia-thalamocortical motor loop
globus_pallidus_left.clinicalRelevance: Dysfunction in this basal ganglia circuit is central to movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease. Educational note, not a diagnostic claim.

globus_pallidus_right.name: Right Globus Pallidus
globus_pallidus_right.location: Deep within the cerebrum, medial to the putamen, part of the basal ganglia.
globus_pallidus_right.summary: A key output structure of the basal ganglia motor circuit.
functions: Part of the basal ganglia-thalamocortical motor loop
globus_pallidus_right.clinicalRelevance: Dysfunction in this basal ganglia circuit is central to movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease. Educational note, not a diagnostic claim.

lateral_ventricle_left.name: Left Lateral Ventricle
lateral_ventricle_left.location: The largest of the brain's ventricles, one within each cerebral hemisphere.
lateral_ventricle_left.summary: C-shaped cavities that produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
functions: CSF production via the choroid plexus
Cushioning and protection of brain tissue
Part of the connected ventricular system

lateral_ventricle_right.name: Right Lateral Ventricle
lateral_ventricle_right.location: The largest of the brain's ventricles, one within each cerebral hemisphere.
lateral_ventricle_right.summary: C-shaped cavities that produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
functions: CSF production via the choroid plexus
Cushioning and protection of brain tissue
Part of the connected ventricular system
